title: Bias and fairness
blurb: How models pick up unfair patterns from the text they learn from.

slides.title: Models learn from human writing — flaws included
body: A model learns from text people have written, and that text reflects the world as it has been described — stereotypes and imbalances included.
The model has no way of telling which patterns are fair. It learns them all, and can repeat them.

visual.caption: A simplified picture of how a bias gets from the data into an answer.

items.label: Training text
items.text: Lots of writing pairs certain jobs with certain genders.

items.label: The model learns
items.text: Those pairings become more likely predictions.

items.label: In its answers
items.text: Stories and suggestions can quietly repeat the stereotype.

slides.title: What it can look like
body: Bias is often subtle. Each answer can look reasonable on its own; the pattern only shows across many answers.
Developers work to reduce this, but it can’t be removed completely.

visual.caption: Example replies written for illustration.
visual.question: Write a short story about a doctor and a nurse.

cards.label: A biased pattern
cards.text: The doctor is always “he” and the nurse is always “she”.

cards.label: A better response
cards.text: The characters vary from story to story, or the story doesn’t assume either.

slides.title: Where else it shows up
body: Bias isn’t only about stereotypes in stories. It can also affect how well a model works for different people.

visual.caption: Some common forms — not a complete list.

items.heading: Uneven quality across languages
items.text: Languages with less training text often get weaker answers.

items.heading: Assumed “default” people
items.text: Assuming a user’s culture, gender or background when it wasn’t mentioned.

items.heading: Skewed judgements
items.text: Rating or ranking people differently based on irrelevant details.

slides.title: What you can do
body: You can’t fix the model, but you can notice bias and stop it reaching decisions that matter.
That matters most when AI output affects real people.

visual.caption: The higher the stakes, the more these matter.

items.heading: Notice the defaults
items.text: Who did the answer assume? Would it change if the details changed?

items.heading: Ask for range
items.text: Prompt for different perspectives, or ask it to avoid assumptions.

items.heading: Keep people in charge
items.text: Decisions about people — hiring, care, access — need human review.

quiz.question: Where does bias in an AI model mainly come from?
options: Patterns in the human-written text it learned from
The model forming its own opinions
quiz.explanation: Models learn patterns from their training data, including unfair ones that appear in human writing.

quiz.question: A model gives better answers in English than in some other languages. What’s the likely reason?
options: It was trained on far more English text
quiz.explanation: Models tend to do best in the languages they saw most during training, and English usually dominates.

quiz.question: AI is used to help screen job applicants. What’s the most important safeguard?
options: Let the AI make the final decision to save time
Have people review decisions and check for unfair patterns
quiz.explanation: When AI output affects people, human review and checking outcomes across groups help catch bias before it does harm.
